FixtureCorp released Aurora on August 15, 2026, a benchmark harness for comparing AI coding assistants across four languages, and the headline claim -- a 32% average score jump over its previous tool, Prism -- is independently reproducible for the first time, unlike Prism's contested 2025 numbers. This matters for engineering teams choosing between assistants, because Aurora is the first harness in this space whose methodology and raw run logs are both published for outside review.

## What FixtureCorp announced

FixtureCorp's [official Aurora announcement](https://fixturecorp.example/blog/aurora-launch) describes Aurora as an open benchmark harness that runs a fixed suite of 220 real-world coding tasks across Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust, then scores completions with a mix of unit-test pass rate and a secondary "maintainability" rubric. The company says Aurora replaces Prism, its 2025 benchmark that [drew criticism from independent reviewers](https://fixturecorp.example/blog/prism-retrospective) for withholding its scoring rubric.

Unlike Prism, Aurora ships with a [public GitHub repository containing every task, every model transcript, and the scoring code itself](https://fixturecorp.example/docs/aurora-methodology), which is the detail most likely to determine whether the wider developer community actually trusts the numbers this time.

## The numbers, and what they measure

FixtureCorp's own leaderboard shows an average pass-rate improvement of 32% across the four tracked assistants when re-scored under Aurora versus their original Prism scores. That is a large jump, and it deserves the same scrutiny FixtureCorp is now inviting: the [company's benchmark data page](https://fixturecorp.example/data/aurora-leaderboard) publishes per-task results, which lets outside teams re-run a subset of tasks rather than trust the aggregate number alone.

| Track | Prism 2025 score | Aurora 2026 score | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 61% | 79% | +18 pts |
| TypeScript | 58% | 74% | +16 pts |
| Go | 49% | 70% | +21 pts |
| Rust | 44% | 68% | +24 pts |

The Rust track shows the largest jump, which FixtureCorp attributes to Prism's older task set containing several ambiguous prompts that Aurora's task-review process caught and rewrote, according to [FixtureCorp's methodology page](https://fixturecorp.example/docs/aurora-methodology). That is a plausible explanation, but it is FixtureCorp's own explanation, and independent verification is exactly what the public repository is supposed to make possible.

## What it means

**For teams picking a coding assistant, Aurora is a better starting point than Prism was, but not a finish line.** A published methodology and raw logs let you check whether a benchmark actually resembles your own codebase's problems before trusting its ranking -- Aurora clears that bar, Prism did not. The sensible use of Aurora's numbers is as a shortlist filter, then a team's own small internal eval on real repository tasks, not a substitute for one.

**For the benchmark space generally, this is a small but real step toward reproducibility.** Coding-assistant benchmarks have had a credibility problem for two years, largely because vendors published scores without the underlying tasks. Aurora does not fix that industry-wide, but a competitor choosing transparency raises the bar other vendors will increasingly be asked to clear.

## The India angle

FixtureCorp has not announced India-specific pricing or a local office, but Aurora itself is free and open-source, which matters more than usual here: India's developer tooling market leans heavily on free and open benchmarks precisely because enterprise procurement budgets for paid evaluation tools are thin outside the largest IT services firms. Indian engineering teams can run Aurora's public suite locally against any assistant they are evaluating, in rupee terms costing only compute time -- no licensing fee, unlike some competing commercial benchmark products. That said, none of Aurora's 220 tasks currently include India-specific coding conventions (regional date/currency formatting, GST-related billing logic), a gap FixtureCorp has not addressed and is worth watching if the harness is adopted locally as a de facto standard.

## What to watch

Three things will determine whether Aurora becomes a genuine industry reference or another vendor benchmark nobody outside FixtureCorp trusts. First, whether outside labs actually re-run the public suite and publish their own numbers in the next few months -- a methodology being open is not the same as it being independently verified. Second, whether FixtureCorp keeps the task set updated as coding assistants improve, since a static benchmark saturates and stops being useful within a year or two. Third, whether competitors publish comparable transparency, or whether Aurora ends up a one-off rather than a new norm. We'll track all three in our [AI Tools coverage](/topics/ai-tools/) as more independent runs land, and revisit this piece if the picture changes.

## FAQ

### What is FixtureCorp Aurora?

Aurora is an open benchmark harness FixtureCorp released on August 15, 2026, for scoring AI coding assistants across Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust using 220 published tasks plus public scoring code.

### Is Aurora free to use?

Yes -- FixtureCorp has not announced any paid tier, and the [public repository](https://fixturecorp.example/docs/aurora-methodology) is openly licensed, so any team can run the suite locally against the assistant of its choice.

### How is Aurora different from Prism?

Prism, FixtureCorp's 2025 benchmark, did not publish its scoring rubric, which drew independent criticism. Aurora publishes its full task set, transcripts and scoring code, letting outside teams re-run and check the results themselves.

Related coverage: our recent look at [how India's IT services firms are adopting AI coding tools](/articles/india-it-ai-coding-tools/) and our [explainer on coding-assistant benchmarks](/articles/ai-coding-benchmarks-explained/) both provide useful background for reading Aurora's numbers in context.
